title: The Glory of the Church and the Gospel of God
english: I make known to you that no one can say 'Lord Jesus' except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor 12:3), and again. 'But the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know, because they are being judged spiritually. But the spiritual man judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one. For who has known the mind of the Lord, which directs him? But we have the mind of Christ' (1 Cor 2:14-16). And again: 'Brothers, if even a man is caught in some transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, watching yourself, lest you also be tempted. Bear one another's burdens, and thus fulfill the law of Christ' (Gal 6:1).

Regarding the reason for the Trinity through their shared essence, what now speaks of the Father, at another time speaks of the Son or of the Holy Spirit. The Scripture, declaring one deity and lordship, now speaks of the Father, and at another time asserts that it is the Son or the Holy Spirit; just as when the uninspired Paul writes to the Philippians: 'For they all seek their own, not those of Jesus Christ' (Phil 2:21), to the Galatians: 'But those of Jesus Christ crucified the flesh with its passions and desires' (Gal 5:24), and to the Corinthians: 'For the love of Christ constrains us, judging this: that he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose for them' (2 Cor 5:14-15). And again: 'But the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him' (1 Cor 2:14); and again: 'But desire the spiritual things' (1 Cor 7:40).

Furthermore, regarding the Church, which is conceived with the glory ascending within it and the bloodless worship being brought to it, writing first to the Corinthians, he announced that it belongs to God thus: 'Become without stumbling to Jews and Greeks and to the Church of God' (1 Cor 10:32), and again: 'We do not have such a custom, nor do the churches of God' (1 Cor 10:33). But writing again to the Ephesians, he taught that it is Christ's, saying thus: 'That he might present to himself the church without blemish, having no spot or wrinkle or anything of this kind, but that it might be holy and immaculate' (Eph 5:27). If—

For since it did not seem so to him here, someone will interpret what the prophet Haggai intends by saying, 'the glory of this house shall be greater than the first' (Haggai 2:9), that is, of the Church of Christ and the glorification within it, compared to the synagogue of the Jews, in which God alone was theologized and glorified.

Therefore also the Gospel, writing to the Romans, says that it is now of God the Father: 'Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, a called apostle, set apart for the gospel of God' (Romans 1:1); and again: 'For I am not ashamed of the gospel: for it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For the righteousness of God is revealed therein; and the just shall live by faith' (Romans 1:16-17); and to the Corinthians the second instance: 'that I preached to you the gospel of God freely' (1 Corinthians 2:4); but in the first instance he writes to the Corinthians that it turns out to be of the only-begotten God: 'but we have not used that authority, but we endure all things, so that we may not cut off anything by the gospel of Christ' (2 Corinthians 10:18); and the second: 'having come into Troas for the gospel of Christ' (Acts 20:7/contextual); and again: 'glorifying God in the submission of your confession unto the gospel of Christ' (2 Corinthians 10:18); and to the Romans: 'For God is my witness, whom I serve in the gospel of His Son' (Romans 15:30).

But he also said that the sacred liturgy is sometimes performed for God the Father and sometimes for God His only-begotten Son, having written to the Corinthians the first: 'Thus let a man reckon us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God; that which is required in stewards, that one be found faithful' (1 Corinthians 4:1-2); the second: 'in everything presenting ourselves as ministers of God' (2 Corinthians 4:5); and again: 'Are they ministers of Christ? I speak foolishly; rather, I do' (1 Corinthians 9:17).

...'Who has believed in the Lord and been encouraged? Or who has endured the fear of Him and been forsaken? Or who has called upon Him and been disregarded?' (Romans 10:9-11). For He, as even those outside say, 'is persuaded by God, and greatly moved by Him.' Therefore, certainly, nothing is unacquired or being worked in oneself by another, from which...

title: The Unity of Glory and Nature
english: He presents all good things as being drawn toward the one divine peace, which has no limit, about which Isaiah cried out: 'Lord our God, give us peace; for you have given us all things. Lord, besides you we know no other' (Isa 26:3). This is given by Him through His power because of the shared nature and lordship. He said: 'Peace I leave with you, my peace I give to you' (John 14:27).

Therefore, Paul also did not fail to provide this God-giving word to both the unbegotten hypostases without distinction (Rom 1:7), writing thus to the Romans: 'Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.' We are also provided the recognition of this in the same way by that: 'All that the Father has is mine' (John 16:15).

For these things are not understood ignorantly regarding creation, but are understood regarding the divine worth, if one is to say they belong to God. For the Father, he says, is God. I am also; for he is his only-begotten, true, and beloved Son. The Father is Lord. I am also lord of all and heir of the living Father, possessing the inheritance. And I inherit his own things, this as the maker of them, and this also as a genuine Son. And I was made heir as one having become man.

The Father is Creator and King. I am. For I said to you as, 'There was a king who went out to make marriages for his son the king' (Matt 22:2). The Father is unchangeable. I am also. For it has been prophesied concerning me: 'You are the same, and your years shall not fail' (Ps 70:5). The Father is impassible. I am, so as to let those who share in me partake of impassibility.

The Father is without beginning. I am. For there was not a time when the hypostatic radiance did not have the name of the Father and of his glory, and the 'character of the hypostasis' and the 'image of the deity,' which is me. Life and light and goodness and power and wisdom and truth and whatever is worthy of God, the Father is. I am, as you have heard by those who have perished.

And indeed I am also Savior, 'raising the sun upon the righteous and the sinners' (Matt 5:45) and not bringing 'evil for evil.' The Father is Philanthropic. I am, wherefore for your sake 'I emptied myself, having taken the form of a slave' (Phil 2:7), and being struck and spat upon and mocked and crucified by you.

We were not misled. All the things he said happen to be in accordance with the Fathers, so that he gives nothing more to God the Father than only being the father of a co-ruling and co-existing Son. Thus he persuades one to believe also that: 'All that is mine is yours, and all that is yours is mine, and I have been glorified in them' (John 17:10).

For if it were not said thus through the natural relation, and if the Son had not been essentially glorified in all the Fathers, unless kingdom and lordship are one, then—according to the logic—it would be heretical, that there is something accomplished not by the authority of the Father, but by the authority of the Son. And again: 'If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing; it is my Father who glorifies me' (John 17:5).

He says, speaking about his own divine glory, that 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30), do not disbelieve; rather, there is the Father witnessing for me, that according to nature I am glorified, being his beloved and true Son, yet [being] God and Lord of you. Then he says: 'Father, glorify your Son, so that your Son also may glorify you' (John 17:5). Equal honor and glory have been preserved thus for the divine hypostases. For in whatever way we conceive of the Father glorifying his Son, by that same way he himself is glorified by him.

And he proceeds again: 'And now glorify me, Father, with the glory I had with you before the world existed' (John 17:5). It is terrible to hear, that he who has glory independently from his own Father—for this is what it means: to have had glory before the world existed—is not glorified according to the heretics. And what was this [glory]? Which, as I think, Mark also said: 'When the Son comes in the glory of his Father' (Mark 8:38), instead of: he possesses the Father's glory and in it he will come a second time.

Of which glory, being one, divinity, kingdom, and worship have been established, not one and another. Therefore he commands beforehand: 'Believe in God, and believe in me. In my Father's house there are many mansions' (John 14:1-2). He says, 'that they may know one faith concerning the Trinity, not having a difference of divinity, so that you may dwell in those three-blessed courts, all in harmony and sufficiency.'
Not only, indeed, those he led, but also, providing [things] of God, he says: 'Your sins are forgiven you' (Luke 7:48). You pay attention likewise to his authority, that as if...

title: Equality of Father and Son
english: He does not act as an ambassador to a greater one, but forgives like an autocrat.

Matthew, contributing himself to the theologies concerning the only-begotten Son, said: 'No one knows the Father except the Son, nor does anyone know the Son except the Father' (Matt 11:27). How then do these people contend as if they knew the Father to be incomparable, his Son to be unlike him, and the essence to be unbegotten? They leave nothing exceptional in the knowledge of God the Father and the only-begotten God, nor do they consider that one who possesses nothing of a different nature possesses knowledge equal to the homoousion. Paul similarly writes to Timothy in the first epistle: 'I charge you before God who gives life to all things and Jesus Christ who bore the good confession in the presence of Pontius Pilate, to guard the unblemished command, without reproach, until the appearing of the Lord Jesus Christ, which the blessed and only powerful one and King of kings and Lord of lords, the only one having immortality and dwelling in unapproachable light, whom no man has seen or is able to see, to whom be honor and glory for the ages of ages. Amen' (1 Tim 1:17).

For it has seemed fitting to the heretics to give this to the Father alone: 'the only powerful one and King of kings' and the following. Just as regarding both of the eternal hypostases he said: 'I charge you before God and Christ Jesus,' so he sang regarding both of them as one in divinity and the following. For he did not ignore like these: 'all that the Father has is mine' (John 16:15), and: 'that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father' (John 5:23), and: 'this is the true God and eternal life' (1 John 5:20), and: 'this is our God; no other shall be reckoned against him' (Isa 42:8), and: 'this is my beloved Son' (Matt 3:17).

But rather, the things set forth are directed more toward the Son. For it says: 'to guard the command until the appearing of the Lord Jesus Christ, which the blessed and only powerful one will show in his own times.' It is clear, therefore, that the Son will show his own appearance when he comes a second time. Thus, it allows that he also grant him the first glory. To the Romans: 'for his invisible things from...'

The eternal power and divinity of the one understood through the works of the world as being created. Because of the equal value of Father and Son, it does not fall short toward a creature. For the eternity and divinity of the Creator is not to be understood in the Begotten; that is, the divinity possessing the same things always. Regarding the Philippians: 'who, existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be snatched, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave' (Phil 2:6).

What of this equality is found unequal? For he did not snatch, he says, he did not take to be equal in nature to God and Father. And indeed, he who was not emptied by another, but having emptied himself, simultaneously showed himself to be a Master and eternal. For if he became in the form of a slave, it is indisputable that he did not remain so, but before this happened, he was in the free paternal nature, in creatures. Since it was not possible to be seen, he descended unchangeably and invisibly until the form of a servant. And he cast off the things of the servant and gave the beginning of a more radiant life; whence and he who was without beginning was known.

And the other things sent to the same Philippians, that he already somehow holds the Son before and above his his own Father as far as he decides toward the irrational, it has already been spoken to me additionally in Chapter 7. And nothing prevents setting this up from the ancient Scripture; for it is necessary not to use theology as a pastime. Therefore God says through Isaiah: 'My soul hates your new moons and your Sabbaths and your feasts. Let them be for me a stench; I will no longer bear your sins. Even if you fill out the prayer, I will not listen to you; for your hands are full of blood. Wash yourselves, make yourselves clean, take away your sins from your souls' (Isa 1:15-16).

You see, then, that even philanthropy reaches the threat, insofar as he is not yet exchanging [them] and not being angry for a long time, but rather not knowing how to be angry at all. And he hates their feasts, which is the religion, as being left behind from the most perfect knowledge of God; and he is exhorted to be baptized so as to receive the faith toward the masterly boundary concerning baptism. And Paul also has assured us elsewhere, having cried out by word, not...
